newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Apartheid army chief free, S.African wounds reopen.
newsitem.headline: Apartheid army chief free, S.African wounds reopen.

text.p: Former hardline defence minister Magnus Malan, the highest-ranking figure of the old white regime to stand trial for atrocities against blacks, was found not guilty of murder on Friday and set free.
In the most important trial of South Africa's post-apartheid era, Malan and others accused of masterminding and carrying out the 1987 killing of 13 blacks, including six children, were acquitted.
The defendants ranged from white army generals to black policemen accused of gunning down the victims with AK-47 assualt rifles.

All faced identical charges of murder, conspiracy to murder and attempted murder for a massacre allegedly carried out by blacks -- foes of Nelson Mandela's African National Congress -- who had been armed by the state to further its divide-and-rule policy.
The impact of the judge's ruling on South Africa's attempts at reconciliation to heal racial wounds was immediate.
Friends of the old regime cheered, supporters of the ANC -- whose activist was supposed to have been killed in the attack -- were stunned.
"All who believe in democracy can gain hope from today's decision, truth has prevailed," said Malan, 66, who led the white regime's war on its black opponents in the 1980s.
The stern-faced pensioner who led the armed forces before joining P.W. Botha's cabinet thanked President Mandela, who he said had let them defend themselves in a court of law.

Anti-apartheid activists said it seemed the "big fish" of the old regime were going to get off scot-free for the misery they wrought while their henchmen, such as police hit-man Eugene de Kock, were jailed.
The ANC, which has long accused the old government of waging a dirty war using a shadowy third force against its foes, said it was dismayed the prosecution methods had seemed so weak.
Mandela moved swiftly to calm angered blacks, for whom Malan was a hate-figure blamed for stoking the violence, much of it between blacks, that terrorised them in apartheid's dying years.
He urged them to respect the much criticised judicial system -- which does not use juries -- and not to give up hope of catching the murderers and paymasters of the past.

"Where people have died as a result of atrocities we will continue to investigate who was responsible and who, in regard to alleged third force activities, was responsible for directing these activities," Mandela said in a statement.

The trial was a landmark in South Africa's attempts to clear up its past, but Judge Jan Hugo said the prosecution had presented a sloppy case that failed to prove who had done the killings or who had pulled the strings.
The United Nations declared apartheid a crime against humanity but it is not on any statute books.

To bring a case state prosecutors had to home in on one of countless incidents involving murders that were crimes even under the old order. The 1987 massacre of a family and church friends turned into a symbol of apartheid's evil.
The state claimed that six black police, members of Zulu chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi's Inkatha Freedom Party, gunned down the 13 in KwaMakutha township near the port of Durban.

Hugo said Inkatha members, armed and trained secretly by the South African military to fight their common foe in the black liberation movement, had doubtless carried out the attack, but not necessarily the six in the dock.
The state claimed that the planning for and blessing of the death squad went right up the ladder to Malan, but the judge said there was no evidence the military had plotted the attack.
Hugo quoted Lewis Carroll and Shakespeare to justify his ruling that the term "offensive groups", mentioned in top-secret apartheid documents, did not imply death squads.
As well as ripping open old apartheid wounds the eight-month trial has sharpened animosity between the ANC and Inkatha, whose deputy secretary-general was among those on trial.
Some 15,000 people have died in a decade of warfare, which is now easing, between the two groups for control of communities in Inkatha's power base of KwaZulu-Natal province.
Senior Inkatha figures said the trial had been politically motivated and that it was now time to put ANC members on trial for the murder of Inkatha supporters.
